technique: scale — moving between the tiny and the large in a few lines
lesson: Today we work on one technique. Call it scale. Scale means the poem moves between something small and something large within a few lines, so you feel both sizes at once. This poem does it quietly. Look at "the laces still looped the way your hands left them." That is small. You are looking at one knot. Then look at "glass holding what the summer made you earn." That is large. A whole season is now sitting in a few jars. Then it goes small again: "the floorboards talk the cold back up through your soles." The change in size makes you pay attention, because your mind has to adjust each time. Small makes a thing exact. Large makes it matter. Try this: put one tiny detail and one big stretch of time in the same stretch of lines. The second time through, listen for how the jars hold the whole summer. Here is the poem.
poem:
The boots by the door stand where you stepped out of them,
mud gone to stone overnight, the laces still looped
the way your hands left them, patient as tools are patient.
Beside them the row of jars catches the window,
each one numbered now, counted, standing its ground,
glass holding what the summer made you earn.
You lace up without looking, fingers knowing the work,
and the floorboards talk the cold back up through your soles.
A long day leans in the frame of the door,
ordinary and waiting, the way good days wait—
not grand, just needing a man who'll stand and meet them.

There's a line waiting in your hands today—
rise, and go set it flowing.
